name: Arisi Paruppu Sadam

ingredients.name: Parboiled rice (puzhungal arisi; raw ponni rice also used)

equipment: Small pressure cooker (1.5 to 2 litre): cooks the rice and dal together
Bowl for soaking, strainer, chopping board and knife, measuring spoons, kitchen scale

steps.title: Rinse the rice and dal
steps.text: Put 65 g rice and 22 g toor dal in a bowl, add water, swirl, and pour the water off. Repeat 2 times.
steps.visualCue: The rinse water turns from milky to nearly clear after 2 to 3 washes
steps.cameraCheck: The rinsed rice and dal in the bowl
steps.videoShot: Water swirling cloudy then clearing over the rice and dal.
steps.watchOut: Rubbing hard, which breaks the grains into fragments and makes the sadam pasty; swirl gently with your fingers instead.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Cover with 1 cup of fresh water and leave for 30 min.
steps.visualCue: The rice turns opaque white and the dal looks slightly plumper and paler
steps.watchOut: Skipping the soak, which leaves the dal firm after 3 whistles; if short of time, use hot water and soak 15 min.
steps.funFact: Cook Click N Devour notes that authentic versions use parboiled rice, and that the dish is less mushy than sambar rice (search snippet).

steps.title: Peel and chop the shallots and garlic
steps.text: Slice 25 g shallots into thin pieces and chop 5 g garlic small.
steps.visualCue: Even thin shallot slices and a small pile of chopped garlic with a sharp smell
steps.cameraCheck: The shallots and garlic on the board
steps.watchOut: Large garlic pieces that stay raw while the rest cooks; chop them small.

steps.title: Chop the tomato
steps.text: Cut 40 g tomato into small pieces.
steps.visualCue: Small red pieces, juicy but not watery
steps.watchOut: Big chunks that will not melt into the masala; chop small so they mash easily in step 10.

steps.title: Heat the ghee
steps.text: Put the cooker (without lid) on medium heat and add 8 g (2 tsp) ghee. Warm for 30 sec.
steps.visualCue: The ghee melts fully, turns clear and smells nutty
steps.cameraCheck: The cooker base with melted ghee
steps.videoShot: Ghee melting into a shimmering pool.
steps.watchOut: Smoking ghee, which turns bitter; if it smokes, lift the cooker off the heat for 20 sec.

steps.title: Temper the mustard and cumin
steps.text: Add 1 g mustard seeds and 1 g cumin seeds. Wait until they crackle.
steps.visualCue: Mustard seeds pop and jump within 10 seconds, and the cumin darkens slightly and smells toasty
steps.cameraCheck: The seeds popping in the cooker
steps.watchOut: Seeds that stay silent (ghee not hot enough) or turn black at once (too hot); wait a few seconds if silent, and lift the pan off the heat if they scorch.

steps.title: Add the curry leaves
steps.text: Add 5 curry leaves and stir for 10 sec.
steps.visualCue: The leaves crackle and curl, and the smell turns herby
steps.watchOut: Water on the leaves, which makes the ghee spit; make sure they are dry.

steps.title: Cook the shallots and garlic
steps.text: Add the shallots, garlic and a pinch of the salt. Stir on medium heat for 3 min.
steps.visualCue: Shallots turn translucent, then light golden, and smell sweet
steps.watchOut: Garlic that browns and turns bitter; keep stirring and add 1 tbsp water if it colours too fast.

steps.title: Add the powders
steps.text: Lower the heat. Add 0.5 g turmeric and 3 g sambar powder and stir for 15 sec.
steps.visualCue: The mix turns deep orange and smells warm and toasty
steps.cameraCheck: The orange masala in the pan
steps.videoShot: Sambar powder dusting into the ghee.
steps.watchOut: Powders that stick and burn with a sharp acrid smell; add the tomato right away or 1 tbsp water to rescue it.

steps.title: Cook the tomato
steps.text: Add the chopped tomato and cook 2–3 min, mashing it with the spoon.
steps.visualCue: The tomato melts into a thick pulp and ghee gathers faintly at the edges
steps.watchOut: Tomato still in sour chunks; mash it with the back of the spoon and cook 1 min more.

steps.title: Add the rice, dal and water
steps.text: Drain the soaked rice and dal and add them to the cooker. Add 240 ml water and the rest of the 2 g salt. Stir once and taste the water, which should taste lightly salty.
steps.visualCue: The water is level with or just above the grains, orange from the masala
steps.cameraCheck: The cooker with water and grains before closing
steps.videoShot: Rice and dal sliding into the masala.
steps.watchOut: Too little water, which leaves the centre of the rice chalky (add 2 tbsp more at once if the grains are above the water); too much water makes the sadam mushy.

steps.title: Pressure cook for 3 whistles
steps.text: Close the lid, fit the weight and cook on medium heat until 3 whistles, then switch off.
steps.visualCue: A steady whistle and steam jet from the vent three times
steps.watchOut: High heat, which scorches the bottom (a burnt smell is the sign); use medium and count whistles. Opening early gives hard dal.

steps.title: Rest until the pressure drops
steps.text: Leave the cooker untouched for 10 min, until the pressure releases on its own.
steps.tip: Cooking for the full 10 min of resting finishes the dal gently, so you do not need a fourth whistle.
steps.visualCue: The steam stops and the pressure pin drops
steps.cameraCheck: The cooker with the pin down
steps.watchOut: Forcing the lid open under pressure, which splits the grains and can spray hot steam; wait for the pin to drop.

steps.title: Fluff and finish
steps.text: Open the lid, stir gently with a fork and sprinkle 2 g chopped coriander. Add a few extra drops of ghee if you like.
steps.visualCue: Moist, tender, separate grains with soft dal, a pale orange colour and a ghee and sambar-powder smell
steps.cameraCheck: The fluffed sadam in the cooker
steps.watchOut: Heavy stirring, which breaks the grains into paste; use a fork and fold lightly. If it is too dry, sprinkle 1–2 tbsp hot water and rest 2 min.
steps.funFact: The dish is popularly nicknamed "kavundar biryani", a nickname tied to the Kongu community (search snippet; see section 12).

reasons: a one-pot meal with about 10 g of protein from rice plus dal, a little ghee (8 g), no frying and no added sugar. Points off for the low vegetable content (only shallot and tomato), a high-carb plate (about 70 g, mostly white parboiled rice), and sodium of about 810 mg (41% of the daily limit). Restaurant or mess versions commonly use more ghee or oil and extra salt, and are served with fried sides such as potato fry and papad (est.).

researchRating.basis: a well-loved Kongu home-style lunch published by many Tamil food blogs (Subbu's Kitchen showed 4.65 from 14 votes in a search snippet), praised as simple, quick and comforting; points off because versions vary a lot (ghee or oil, dal ratio, whether it is spicy or mild), the votes seen were few, and it is rarely sold in restaurants outside Tamil Nadu. Star counts for other sites were not checked. Platform dish ratings were not used.

storage: Fridge-safe in a closed box for up to 1 day (cool within 1 hour; cooked rice and dal should not sit out). Freezing is not recommended (the rice turns hard and grainy). Reheat in a pan or microwave with 2–3 tbsp water until steaming hot.
leftoverRemix: Paruppu sadam cutlets. Mash the cold leftover with 1 tbsp besan or rice flour and a little chopped coriander, shape into small patties and shallow-fry on a tawa with 1 tsp oil until golden on both sides.
burnOff: about 5.9 km of running (410 ÷ 70 kcal/km, for a 70 kg adult), or about 8.2 km of brisk walking (about 1 h 38 min at 5 km/h, using about 50 kcal/km for walking) (est.).

navratri.reason: rice, toor dal, shallot, garlic and table salt are all outside the common vrat rule set (assumption: common rule set; families differ).

ekadashi.reason: the dish is built on rice and dal (grain and pulse), avoided on Ekadashi under the common rule set.

jain.reason: shallot and garlic are roots; drop both and use hing and sonth (dry ginger powder), see the Jain variant.

ramadan.reason: vegetarian, no halal-meat issue; about 810 mg sodium (est.), filling at sehri with curd or raita and fine as a light iftar dinner.

jain.reason: the main recipe uses shallot and garlic (roots); cook the Jain variant (no shallot or garlic, hing and sonth).

vegan.reason: the main recipe tempers in ghee; use the Vegan variant (oil instead of ghee, as Sharmi's Passions does).

pescatarian.reason: vegetarian, so no meat or egg; no fish needed.

sattvik.reason: the main recipe uses shallot 25 g and garlic 5 g; cook the Sattvik variant.

glutenFree.reason: rice, toor dal, ghee and spices only; the recipe uses no hing. Check the sambar powder label for added flour; most hing sold in India is compounded with wheat flour, so use gluten-free hing if you add any.

dairyFree.reason: ghee is dairy; use the Dairy-free variant (oil instead of ghee).
